title: Solihull father paralysed after diving into paddling pool - BBC

 Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Family's 'worst nightmare' after dad paralysed diving into paddling pool
 9 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Rachael Lewis , West Midlands and Sarah Julian , BBC Radio WM Brogan Sam was playing in a new paddling pool with his children when he was seriously injured As temperatures began to soar during the late May bank holiday, Brogan and her family - like many others - were looking for ways to make the most of the weather. 
 Her husband Sam, 38, went out to the shops to buy his family a large paddling pool for their garden in Solihull, filling it up straight away for their children to use. 
 But what was supposed to be a weekend of playing out in the sun became what Brogan has described as her family's worst nightmare, after Sam dived in and struck the bottom of the pool headfirst. 
 "He was face down in the water," Brogan recalled. "When I turned him over, I realised this was an emergency. 
 "He was starting to go blue, he wasn't breathing, that's when panic set in."
 Brogan Sam's injuries have left him unable to move from the neck down An ambulance was called, and the football coach was taken to hospital, where the family were told he had broken bones in his neck and suffered a spinal cord injury.
 Six months later, Sam's injuries have left him unable to move from the neck down, and he remains at a specialist spinal injuries hospital unit in Oswestry, Shropshire - an hour-and-a-half drive from the couple's home. 
 "I go every day, then come back and do bed time with the children," Brogan said. "We have been living with my parents since this happened.
 "The children haven't been able to go back into the house, we have tried over the summer holidays. But when we go back, their dad isn't there."
 Sam has since been having four hours of physiotherapy and occupational therapy each week, with the family now raising money to try and pay for further private sessions.
 Brogan Brogan and Sam have been together since they were 15 "The physios [and] the nurses at the hospital are incredible, so kind, you can tell that is their vocation," Brogan continued.
 "There has been progress, Sam is starting to get some function back with his arms. He is starting to get sensation back across his body. If you're touching him, he can feel that."
 The family is also raising money to make adaptations to their home, as it is currently inaccessible for a wheelchair user. 
 Sam's brother Tom, said: "The family home is not set up for someone who is currently in a wheelchair, who would likely need a bedroom downstairs, 
 "There is a huge amount of work that would need to be done on the house."
 "We need to make it as accessible as we can, to make sure Sam can still be part of family life," Brogan added.
